methodology.title: Curated source-first AI intelligence brief
methodology.summary: This dataset is generated from public source feeds. Items are linked back to their original URLs, timestamped, and auto-categorized for triage rather than treated as infallible truth.
caveats: Feed freshness depends on source publication latency and RSS availability.
Threads coverage uses RSSHub adapters and may fail or lag if the upstream route changes.
Automatic categorization is heuristic and should be reviewed for decision-critical workflows.

research.title: RL Post-Training in Diffusion Transformers Is Activation Steering
research.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) post-training substantially improves the visual quality, text rendering, and compositional accuracy of diffusion transformers. Because capabilities such as rendering requested text or composing multiple objects are inherently prompt-dependent, a natural hypothesis is that improving them requires learning complex, input-dependent transformations. To isolate how much of these gains an input-independent shift explains, we probe each RL-tuned model with a deliberately simple parameterization: a fixed set of steering vectors added to the block outputs of the frozen base model. On SD3.5-M, these vectors hold 65x fewer parameters than the RL-tuned LoRA (0.29M against 18.8M). We fit them to match the velocity predictions of public RL-tuned checkpoints, with no reward in the objective. Although the vectors are identical for every prompt, token, and sampling seed, they recover 90.0-96.3% of the reward gains of six RL-tuned image models, and 89.8% and 111.9% on two RL-tuned video models. Initialized at zero and trained with online RL, the vectors alone exceed the reward gains of weight-based RL on text rendering (OCR) and human preference (PickScore) on SD3.5-M. A constant shift thus suffices for most of the gain of policy-gradient RL post-training: without new input-dependent transformations, it steers the pretrained generator toward what it can already compute.

research.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience
research.summary: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.

research.title: TideCache: Efficient Hybrid LLM Serving with Transparent Cache Management and Layer-Wise Streaming
research.summary: Hybrid architectures have become mainstream among open-weight language models. Their global-attention and bounded-state layers maintain heterogeneous caches whose demands vary with context length and concurrency. We present TideCache, a serving system on CPU--GPU superchips with three components for allocating GPU memory among caches and managing their residency across GPU and host memory. The Transparent Cache Pool redistributes physical pages among cache components behind fixed virtual addresses, preserving cache layouts and backend interfaces. The Cache Streamer uses computation intervals provided by bounded-state layers to prefetch the next global-attention layer's prefix into GPU slots shared across global-attention layers, reducing GPU residency while overlapping layer-wise transfers with computation. Generated KV remains resident. The Request Scheduler selects resident or streamed execution and triggers capacity adjustments according to request size and queue state. Together, they let HBM released by streaming accommodate other cache components and additional requests. Implemented in SGLang and evaluated on GB300 and GH200 across seven model/platform configurations, TideCache completes up to 2.04x as many agent turns, reduces overall P50 per-token latency by 20--59%, and improves agent P50 TTFT by 1.40--3.05x compared with SGLang with HiCache.

research.title: One Prior, Two Dynamics: Repurposing Video Diffusion Transformers for Self-Supervised Latent Action Learning
research.summary: Videos reveal how the world changes, but rarely the actions that cause those changes. Latent action learning recovers such supervision from visual transitions, yet often learns the underlying dynamics largely from scratch. We ask whether a pretrained video generator can instead provide the prior for both inverse and forward dynamics. We introduce O$^{2}$LaF, built on a simple principle: one prior, two dynamics. We initialize both models from the same pretrained video DiT and adapt them to their distinct roles: a feed-forward transition encoder with learnable action queries for inverse dynamics, and a causal, action-conditioned video generator for forward dynamics. By controlling information access and optimizing both dynamics end-to-end through a compact bottleneck, O$^{2}$LaF learns transferable actions from unlabeled videos. Across navigation and robotic manipulation, O$^{2}$LaF sets a new state of the art in few-shot action probing and enables stronger zero-shot action transfer across visual contexts and embodiments. Beyond generative video priors, we further extend our framework to predictive representation priors such as V-JEPA2, achieving competitive performance. Our findings suggest a broader paradigm for latent-action learning: repurposing pretrained video models to discover transferable actions and predict their consequences.

research.title: AgentRoboCritic: Understanding the Capability of Frontier Agents on Direct Robot Control
research.summary: Frontier multimodal language agents such as GPT-6 Astra have demonstrated strong capabilities in controlling robots directly via low-level numerical actions without high-level primitives. However, existing benchmarks report only episode-level success rates, which show neither how these agents succeed nor where they fail. In this paper, we present a systematic action-level analysis of frontier agents on direct robot control across 12 manipulation benchmarks. We introduce AgentRoboCritic, an intent-grounded critique framework in which the policy agent states a local intent alongside each action, and a critic evaluates the action's outcome and failure mode against this intent. Our action-level analysis demonstrates the promising capabilities of frontier agents on direct robot control, including closed-loop recovery from local execution failures, reliable semantic grounding across diverse scenes, and strong zero-shot manipulation without task-specific adaptation. It also identifies their current limitations, including task-relevant physical execution bottlenecks such as grasping and alignment, and uneven recovery across failure modes. Finally, we validate our critic on a 400-action human-annotated benchmark and release a dataset of 12,844 annotated actions alongside a fine-tuned open-source critic, Muse-Glimmer-30B, whose failure-mode accuracy rises from 32.58% to 74.24%, enabling low-cost action-level analysis.

research.title: Bio-PM-Guided Synthetic IMU Generation
research.summary: Collecting and labeling inertial measurement unit (IMU) data for human activity recognition (HAR) is expensive, and models trained on one group of subjects often fail to generalize to unseen individuals. Even with balanced data, classifiers struggle to distinguish dynamically similar activity classes and benefit from targeted augmentation. We explore whether synthetic IMU data generated in the representation space of a pretrained biosignal encoder, Bio-PM \cite{b1}, can serve as a practical augmentation source. Rather than synthesizing raw signals, we leverage Bio-PM's frozen encoder to convert 10-second IMU windows into token embedding sequences and train class-conditional decoders in this space: (1) an autoregressive transformer decoder that predicts tokens sequentially, and (2) a diffusion decoder that learns the token distribution through a denoising objective. We analyze generation realism through distributional metrics and embedding-space visualizations, evaluate downstream utility through leave-one-subject-out HAR classification, and present a PatchDecoder for approximate raw waveform reconstruction. Our diffusion decoder achieves a Train-on-Synthetic-Test-on-Real (TSTR) macro-F1 of 0.68, demonstrating that generated tokens are realistic enough to train a classifier that transfers to real data. Combining synthetic-token augmentation with a 320-dimensional gravity-aware feature representation raises LOSO macro-F1 from 0.729 to 0.809 over a real-only baseline across 51 subjects on the WISDM benchmark, with statistically significant gains concentrated in the most challenging activity classes. These results demonstrate that high-fidelity generation in a pretrained encoder's representation space is achievable and practically useful for cross-subject HAR augmentation.

research.title: Depth Pro 2: Sharp and Temporally Consistent Metric Monocular Depth
research.summary: We present Depth Pro 2, an approach to estimating dense metric depth for images and video at full resolution. By analyzing prior methods for monocular depth estimation, we find that they commonly trade off temporal consistency and boundary sharpness: multi-frame methods favor consistency, single-frame methods favor sharpness. To overcome this trade-off, we train a single, scalable network that processes both images and video and predicts depth maps at native resolution. Depth Pro 2 produces depth maps that are metrically accurate, sharp, and temporally consistent all at once, outperforming prior work in all of these dimensions. We release a family of models that define a new Pareto frontier in terms of metric accuracy, sharpness, temporal consistency, and runtime. We release code and weights at https://apple-aiml-research.github.io/ml-depth-pro-2/

research.title: SoK: Assessing the Evolution of LLM Capability in Software Vulnerability Research
research.summary: LLM-based agents are becoming increasingly capable at discovering, validating and patching vulnerabilities in real software, and vendors and researchers report that this is already changing how vulnerabilities are found and fixed. These claims, however, are scattered across papers, vendor reports and disclosures and are rarely comparable. We introduce a framework that rates these capabilities on an autonomy scale modeled on the levels of driving automation, and qualifies each claim by its correctness, its availability and the strength of its evidence. We use this framework to systematize the published evidence on LLM capability in vulnerability research. We find that agents discovered, validated, and patched vulnerabilities in real-world software without human intervention before the restricted frontier models of 2026, and that open-weight models subsequently attained comparable autonomy for discovery and validation. We then measure the consequences of evolving LLM security capabilities in a decade of public vulnerability records, advisories and exploitation data. In 2026 the number of disclosed vulnerabilities more than doubled, with an increasing share rated critical or high, and severe bugs that had survived a decade or more in widely used code were reported several times more often than before. Yet the time between the stages of a vulnerability's life, from report to fix and from disclosure to attack, has not shifted noticeably so far. We grade the mitigations proposed in the literature with an explicit rubric and draw guidance for each group of stakeholders from the best-supported ones.

research.title: Active Feature Acquisition by Distilling an Oracle Teacher
research.summary: Acquiring every feature of an instance is often costly: a measurement can carry a monetary price, a time delay, or a privacy cost. Active Feature Acquisition (AFA) addresses this by learning a policy that decides, per instance, which features to acquire under a budget. Existing AFA methods train this policy by optimizing a self-constructed utility target rather than distilling an explicit teacher. We construct this teacher explicitly. At training time the label and the unobserved feature values are available, and together they determine the teacher in closed form: an oracle that ranks every candidate by its effect on the downstream predictor's error. OracleImitator distills this ranking into a deployable policy by soft-target imitation. Across multimodal medical diagnosis and the AFABench benchmark, OracleImitator matches or outperforms existing AFA methods across the budget range, recovering 90% of the attainable accuracy gain at under a quarter of the acquisition cost. Because the teacher is an explicit algorithmic object rather than an implicit optimization target, we can also measure directly how much of its ranking is recoverable by a policy restricted to what is visible at deployment.

research.title: PGX: Physically Grounded Execution for Long-Horizon Humanoid Loco-Manipulation
research.summary: Robotic vision-language-action (VLA) models can execute diverse individual manipulation skills, yet they still struggle with long-horizon loco-manipulation tasks, where temporal structure, skills, and precision are tightly coupled within a monolithic model. We propose Physically Grounded Execution (PGX), a framework that offloads temporal and precision control to two classical training-free components, allowing the VLA to focus on stage-specific skill dynamics. PGX decomposes long-horizon loco-manipulation into three layers: (i) a predicate-based state machine governs task progression, using physical predicates to gate phase transitions, trigger recovery, and coordinate navigation and waiting. Shared predicate semantics connect offline demonstration segmentation, online execution, and stage-wise evaluation; (ii) VLA skills operate within active manipulation phases, with flat or stage-trained models concentrating on task-relevant actions; and (iii) world-coordinate locking (WCL) maintains spatial consistency through base station keeping, object-relative positioning, and world-anchored contact targets. We demonstrate the effectiveness of PGX with extensive experiments conducted on three simulated tasks and one real-world task using a Unitree G1 humanoid robot for long-horizon loco-manipulation, showing improvements in stage progression and task success rates. Project page is available at: https://kl-research.github.io/pgx

research.title: Realized versus Population Reliability: Anytime-Valid Self-Consistency Certification under Correlated Reasoning
research.summary: Self-consistency certification treats repeated sampling from a language model as sequential evidence accumulation and stops when an anytime-valid e-process crosses a threshold, guaranteeing finite-sample Type I error control by Ville's inequality. Prior constructions assume sampled rollouts are conditionally independent. We show this assumption fails in practice: reasoning streams are positively correlated through shared reasoning prefixes or across-prompt heterogeneity, changing not merely certificate efficiency but the hypothesis certified. Modeling dependence via a per-unit latent state (the random-effects / intraclass-correlation structure) induces exchangeable, equi-correlated increments with correlation $ρ$. Correlation splits the single null into a realized null about the drawn belief and a population null about average model behavior, which coincide only when $ρ=0$. We show: (i) the standard betting e-process remains anytime-valid for the realized null, not the population null; (ii) read as a population-null test, a suitable mixture has asymptotic crossing probability at least $π=P(μ(Z)>0)$, potentially exceeding nominal $ε$; (iii) the within-unit mean's effective sample size saturates at $1/ρ$, so extra within-unit rollouts cannot restore population validity; and (iv) a prompt-level e-process restores population validity, with optimal allocation at one rollout per prompt under a pure rollout budget. Simulations and Claude Haiku 4.5 rollouts confirm this regime dependence: on GSM8K ($\hatρ=0.435$, $\hatθ=+0.96$) the gap is dormant, whereas on AIME ($\hatρ=0.480$, $\hatθ=-0.15$) the single-unit rule crosses on 24% of prompts at nominal $ε=0.05$, while the prompt-level procedure declines (0.00). This correctness result identifies which reliability claim an anytime-valid certificate actually supports under dependence.

research.title: Probing the "Conscious" Mind: Selective Access and Global Workspace in Vision-Language Models
research.summary: Vision-language models (VLMs) integrate visual and textual information, but their outputs do not reveal internal concept representations. Global workspace theory (GWT) proposes that information is selected from parallel brain processes, integrated in a shared workspace, and made available to specialised processes. We introduce the Multimodal Concept Lens (MC-Lens), a multimodal Jacobian lens, to study these functions in VLM concept processing. Its vision encoder and language decoder lenses map intermediate states to a shared semantic space defined by the decoder's output vocabulary to compare concept accessibility across modalities. MC-Lens supports internal concept interventions to examine the role of accessed concepts in downstream computation. (i) Accessibility and selective access. Multimodal concept information is readable in intermediate states and selectively accessible as tasks require. We extend "readout carriers" from one name token to a token set to better capture and express concept information and support counterfactual experiments. (ii) Concepts in downstream computation. Counterfactual experiments show that accessed concept information participates in downstream computation and reasoning. (iii) Development of cross-modal alignment and selective access. We develop two J-space metrics tracking the development of cross-modal concept alignment more clearly than hidden state cosine in controlled VLM training. The experiment also shows that reliable selective access develops later than concept accessibility. (iv) Shared functions across models. Across VLM families and sizes, we find shared patterns of concept accessibility, query-dependent selectivity and cross-task intervention effects despite differences in internal organisation. These findings offer an experimental basis to study GWT in multimodal artificial systems and how it can guide cross-modal alignment improvements.

news.title: Q&A: Enabling more human-like interactions and understanding in multimodal foundation models
news.summary: Humans experience and interact with the world through sensory information. This could mean learning correspondences between the sound of bird chirps and the word “robin,” or being able to visually identify and follow your friend “Sarah” in a crowd of people. In many cases, people are able to draw on their latent “multimodal” knowledge — information across multiple data types, from audio to video to text or spoken word — to perform these tasks without many, or sometimes even any, examples. Multimodal foundation models of artificial intelligence are increasingly gaining capabilities that mimic this. However, their apparent multimodal fluency often belies their actual understanding. An MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab team, co-led by Jim Glass, senior research scientist in the MIT Computer Science and Artificial Intelligence Laboratory, has been investigating critical failures of state-of-the-art multimodal models and developing benchmarks and data-efficient methods to overcome these performance gaps with limited supervision. He speaks about this work in the following interview. Q:  What were your goals for this project, and why would you opt to address AI models’ weaknesses over scaling to larger models?     A: This project has been going on for many years now, with roughly the same MIT-IBM team of speech and vision experts. We've wanted to explore the relationship between perception (things that you see and hear) and language, largely speaking: We have all of this absorbed knowledge and language skills, text-based, in the form of a large language model, so we wanted to know how you can relate them without using a whole bunch of annotated training data. Sometimes the models have seen certain phenomena, a latent representation of something that they have internally, but maybe due to subsequent fine-tuning or something, it disappears, so, developing techniques to try to make this capability re-emerge is a useful thing.  As you study these publicly available models, you can see weaknesses even in big ones, so I think it's important to try to address these limitations. If you had an unlimited budget, you could go out and create the annotations that you need, but it's also good to be able to try to get these models to learn more on their own. We’ve done that by creating novel benchmarks that we can evaluate against, then developing techniques that perform better on these benchmarks, and getting these models to learn on their own. Throughout our research collaboration — and this has very much been a strong collaboration between MIT and IBM — we have continued to release public benchmarks for people to use, and that's a lasting artifact. I think the overriding themes are multimodalities with language models, trying to address the shortcomings of these models, and trying to develop techniques that do not require a lot of annotated data to complete tasks better. Q:  Can you walk us through how the project has evolved? A: When we first started this project, we were trying to build models that could learn correspondences automatically, not telling the machine anything more than, “This audio caption goes with this picture,” sort of like reading a picture book to a child who's learning language. We would just show it these matching examples, and we'd show it mismatching examples. They could learn that the sequence of sounds that says “lighthouse” corresponds to a picture of a lighthouse, without any text being involved. Moving beyond speech was to include general audio, and then we started looking at video instead of still images. We would train the model, showing it matching video sequences with the corresponding audio stream and then mismatching ones, and make it reconstruct them. We would also mask some of the images or the audio, and have the model reconstruct it. The model would learn strong relationships; then, far beyond speech, it would learn what parrots sound like, or electric guitars versus acoustic guitars, for example. Then, when these large language models started coming out — and this was in the early days, before it had been done by the big companies — we started to learn correspondences between audio and language. Since that time, these large multimodal models have become available, and we've started looking at what some of the limitations of these models are, and are trying to improve upon them with these more or less supervised techniques. Q:  What would you say are some recent highlights of your work? A: Our IPLoc research was looking at the fact that these state-of-the-art models, like GPT-40, can't localize specific objects, given just a few-shot examples. We came up with this technique where we would train it with a pseudonym substitution. There's an example there where we replaced “airplane” with “Elizabeth.” It forces the model to not fall back on things that it had previously learned about and pay more attention to the visual context. Then, we had an audio-based paper, OmniR1 , that was looking at audio-large language models, so these are models that can listen to something and talk about them. One of the disturbing things we found is some of these benchmarks are multiple-choice answers . A lot of times, these models aren't really listening to the sound, but they're almost gaming the question by looking at the answer. What animal is roaring in this audio — like a chipmunk, a lion, an alligator, and a chickadee, or something? It's not even really paying attention to the audio, [but] just going, “Oh, lion.” Part of the reason people do that is that it’s simple to evaluate, whereas if you asked for a text response, you’d somehow have to grade whether it’s accurate. Do you get humans to evaluate it, which can be expensive and time-consuming, or do you use some other language model to be the judge that can have its own set of issues as well? One way to address that is to evaluate these models on a variety of different kinds of benchmarks. We realized you could feed random noise, and they were still doing quite well, which shows that they're just paying attention to the question. So, we tried to develop some methods to have it pay more attention to the audio and minimize this behavior. Q:  Given resource constraints, what is your approach to adapting these large foundation models, and what blend of AI and algorithmic methods do you use that don't require extensive annotated data? A: These days, we can't create one of these very large foundation models ourselves. We don't have the resources to do that, so we're tending to use these available models and trying to adapt them, train them in a weakly supervised way, methods that don't require as much data, like our work on test-time reinforcement learning . Our project was not monolithic, in the sense that we're not all working on one thing. It's more like a thousand flowers bloom, so there's no one particular way that we're approaching things. Q:  In the near future, how do you see multimodal research evolving in your MIT-IBM research team? A: Over the years, we probably produced two dozen or so significant collaborative papers, and during this work, it was amazing to me that the machines could learn these correspondences without being told anything. No one had ever shown that machines could do it before we did that. Some of our early work combining audio with large language models was fun, too: seeing the model talk about what it heard and then having a conversation with it. Now, we are starting to take this for granted, but at the time, it was fun to see. Moving forward, for the coming year, with our MIT-IBM collaboration, we're going to switch gears a little bit and focus more on what's known as full-duplex spoken dialogue systems. These are models that are listening while they’re talking, so it’s more like how humans operate, and this is quite different from what we’ve been doing up until now, which is joint audio-visual work, which we will also continue.  Now, we’ll be focusing on the speech side of things. These full-duplex models have suddenly become an interesting thing to look at, because they would move you away from the rigid turn-taking approach that is used right now when you're talking to some of these models. Ultimately, I think they will be more natural to interact with.  These full-duplex models are just starting to emerge, and some of the ones that are publicly available aren't as good as the big, large language models. They can handle some of these low-level communication skills, but they're still missing some things, like the concept of time, or knowledge depth. So, we're working on trying to address some of these issues. This research has been conducted in coordination with the MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab teams of Rogerio Feris , Brian Kingsbury , and Samuel Thomas of IBM Research, and Hilde Kuehne of the University of Tuebingen, who is an MIT-IBM affiliated researche r.
authors: Lauren Hinkel | MIT-IBM Computing Research Lab

news.title: New approach enables physically consistent AI models of chaotic systems
news.summary: Modeling of complex, chaotic processes such as weather and climate patterns and turbulent flows in aviation or in ocean currents has advanced enormously in recent years. However, such models are still prone to drift into physically impossible predictions over time. Now, researchers with MIT’s Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems (LIDS) have found a way to introduce physics-based restrictions on machine learning models that can ensure that such models never exceed realistic bounds, based on what is actually possible in the real world. This new approach, using information that is now being made freely available by the team, could significantly improve the usefulness and reliability of such models, which besides climate and weather are also used in a wide range of industrial processes, aeronautics, and hydrology. The new findings are published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences (PNAS) in a paper by MIT graduate student Sunbochen Tang and MIT professors Navid Azizan and Themistoklis Sapsis.  “Lack of guarantees for a bounded response has always been a major obstacle on formulating data-driven models for complex nonlinear systems,” says Sapsis, a professor of mechanical engineering and LIDS affiliate. The approach the team has developed, he says, “paves the way for applying the most advanced machine-learning architectures for prediction and control in a plethora of real-world problems, even those characterized by intrinsic instabilities.” Developing reliable models for complex dynamical systems is important across many domains. In fluid dynamics, turbulent flows can disrupt air travel, reduce the efficiency of wind turbines, and affect fuel economy of vehicles. Similarly, in weather forecasting, the chaotic nature of atmospheric dynamics makes accurate long-term predictions difficult.  “Tiny differences in the starting conditions can lead to dramatically different outcomes in a chaotic system,” Azizan says. “That makes predicting its behavior far into the future extremely difficult.” And yet, there are always physical constraints on the kinds of changes that are possible in the real world. “Chaos does not mean anything can happen. These systems often remain bounded, and their models should, too.” But how to introduce those boundaries into the models has been a thorny problem, says Azizan, the Hayes Associate Professor in the Department of Mechanical Engineering and the Institute for Data, Systems, and Society, and a principal investigator in LIDS. “A model can match the data over a short period and still fail when you let it run for a long time,” he says. “Small errors can accumulate until the simulation produces values that grow without limit,” producing predictions that could never actually occur in real systems. “It’s a fundamental problem with many of the existing machine learning models,” he says. “It’s a question that comes up frequently in different domains: how can we embed physical constraints into these models in a way that preserves their flexibility, but ensures physically meaningful outputs?” “We want to preserve the chaos without the artificial runaway behavior that the real system does not have,” he says. “Our approach gives the model room to learn complex dynamics while guaranteeing that its trajectories stay bounded.” This is the first work that establishes such formal guarantees for machine learning models of chaos. Previous attempts to prevent unrealistic results from such models have often been based on “imposing penalties or incentives during training,” says Tang, a doctoral student in the Department of Aeronautics and Astronautics and LIDS, using functions that are often designed based on privileged information about the system. But as these only apply during the training process for the model, “there’s no guarantee that the model will satisfy the underlying constraints intended by such incentives at test time” once it is dealing with new inputs when it is actually used. “The model could still produce unbounded predictions,” he says. To illustrate why simply imposing arbitrary limits would not be a satisfactory solution to the prediction stability issue, Tang explains, “you can cap the predictions, for example, by setting an arbitrary limit on physical quantities, such as 100 degrees for temperature. That’s one possible way to keep predictions bounded, but it could restrict the model from representing complex and nontrivial features that should be learned directly from the data.” He says that “what sets our approach apart is that we formulate energy-based constraints. We let the model learn an energy-like function,” based on real-world chaotic systems, where energy dissipation helps keep trajectories bounded despite their complex behaviors. “Specifically, the model learns an energy-like function, along with a boundary where its chaotic behavior should be confined to. We then add a projection layer, a component that adjusts how the model predicts the system will evolve, to enforce energy dissipation as a hard constraint. Outside this boundary, the energy-like quantity must decrease, so the simulated system is drawn toward the bounded region. That way, we can establish theoretical guarantees that the model prediction remains bounded over arbitrarily long forecast windows.” The team tested their approach on a variety of different well-known physical systems, ranging from simple textbook cases to highly complex multidimensional systems, and found that their approach closely matched the true outcomes, while conventional approaches soon deviated into impossible predictions. Azizan adds that “the fundamental difference between our approach and the existing approaches is what we call hard constraining versus soft constraining.” While many of the current approaches “try to incentivize the model to satisfy the constraints, they’re not treated as hard constraints. Our approach is based on the concept of hard-constrained neural networks,” so that what comes out “is always physically consistent, even if it’s a completely new case the model hasn’t seen.” “AI models shine in scenarios where there’s a large amount of data available,” Azizan says, for example with images or with text, both of which are abundantly available on the internet. However, he says, “for a lot of physical systems, data is not as abundant.” For such cases where the data is limited, he says, “these physics-constrained approaches can help a lot, because the physics of the problem is another source of information.” The new approach is broadly useful for any chaotic systems. “This is readily applicable to a wide range of neural network architectures,” Tang says. They plan to continue testing it on ever-larger systems. “We’re trying to see how well this would work on data-driven models of realistic weather systems.” “The projection layer is modular: it is model-agnostic and can work with different neural network architectures,” Azizan says. “We hope other researchers and practitioners will build on it and test it on larger and even more complex problems.” The paper, along with open-source code, is now accessible online at PNAS . A follow-up work this year by members of the team was presented at the Learning for Dynamics and Control conference. The paper won the conference’s Best Paper Award. “Trustworthy and reliable AI needs more than just evidence that a model usually works,” Azizan says. “For high-stakes applications, you need guarantees about the properties that must always hold. In this work, we established one such guarantee: boundedness. Our broader goal is to make principles part of how AI models are built, not just how they are tested.”
authors: David Chandler | Laboratory for Information and Decision Systems

news.title: Following the “mathocalypse,” mathematicians consider the future
news.summary: It’s been a tumultuous year for math. Big open questions that have occupied mathematicians for decades are now being solved in a matter of hours by artificial intelligence agents that companies deploy by the thousands to work on a single problem in tireless lockstep.  AI’s relentless rise is raising existential questions for the field: How will the tools affect humans’ understanding of mathematical concepts? In the face of AI’s brute-force productivity, will mathematicians still have jobs? And what will all this mean for mathematics as an intellectual pursuit?  At MIT, mathematicians grappled with these and other questions at a panel discussion on Monday titled “AI and Society: The Future of Math.” Leading mathematicians from MIT, Harvard University, Northwestern University, and New York University — each experts in their respective fields — sat down for a conversation that touched on the quality of AI math, how AI is challenging long-established research norms, and the evolving opportunities for mathematicians, whether they embrace the machines or remain “AI vegans.” The wide-ranging discussion, which took place in a packed lecture hall in MIT’s Building 3, was moderated by science writer Kevin Hartnett, author of “The Proof in the Code,” and featured Jacopo Borga, the Cecil and Ida Green Career Development Assistant Professor of Mathematics at MIT; Michael Hopkins, the George Putnam Professor of Pure and Applied Mathematics at Harvard University; Bryna Kra, the Sarah Rebecca Roland Professor of Mathematics at Northwestern University; and Tristan Buckmaster, professor of mathematics at New York University's Courant Institute of Mathematical Sciences. As the panelists shared their various and at times conflicting perspectives on AI’s impact, one thing was clear: “Math has changed more in the last two months than in the last 100 years,” said Kra, who cautioned that AI’s power will change what it is to be a mathematician and what it will take to advance human knowledge in meaningful ways. “It’s like the first sentence in ‘A Tale of Two Cities’: ‘It was the best of times, it was the worst of times.’ It’s a really exciting moment … and also scary.” AI’s sprint Artificial intelligence has made steady strides over the last decade thanks in large part to mathematicians themselves, who out of curiosity have been honing AI models to solve problems with known solutions. These early exercises proved successful, most notably in 2025. That summer, at the International Mathematical Olympiad, Google DeepMind’s AI models achieved gold-medal status by quickly finding solutions to most of the problems that were posed to the world’s best high school mathematicians.  Around that same time, other mathematicians found that some AI systems could solve problems with known solutions, but in ways that were slightly improved compared to the solutions that human mathematicians had derived.  In 2026, AI’s power took a quantum leap. In several instances, scientists found that models could solve open-ended research questions — mathematical problems that had no known answer. Then, in September, OpenAI made a field-shaking announcement: The company focused thousands of its AI agents on a singular challenge, and after 88 hours, the agents produced a proof related to the Navier-Stokes equation — a Millienum Prize Problem that is one of seven unsolvable mathematical Holy Grails.  OpenAI’s sudden interest in the Navier-Stokes challenge coincided with work by Tristan Buckmaster, one of the panelists. After a year of progress, he and his collaborator, at rival AI behemoth Anthropic, were on the cusp of solving the problem when OpenAI made its announcement. OpenAI’s sprint to be first to the proof opened up a huge debate, about whether proper credit was given, whether the mathematicians’ data was leaked, how the AI agents arrived at their solution, whether that solution makes any meaningful sense, and above all, how AI will change mathematical research.  A month later, the company doubled down, releasing 722 manuscripts, organized into categories that ran the gamut of mathematical topics. The manuscripts claimed to have used AI entirely to solve many of math’s major, unsolved problems — an achievement that has widely been coined the “mathocalypse.”  But many mathematicians insist that it isn’t just about whether a problem can be solved, but also, how. And, they say, when they’ve looked into the details of AI proofs, it’s not clear how the agents arrived at their conclusions.  “The papers themselves are nonsense,” Hopkins said during Monday’s discussion, noting that AI-generated proofs contain “strange ideas.” He continued: “There still is a sense of AI math versus human math.” “For math to be important, it has to have human understanding,” Buckmaster added.  New norms For mathematicians like Kra, this moment in math’s history presents an opportunity to let go of certain long-held norms of mathematical research, such as competition among research groups and the prestige of being the first to prove an idea, also known as priority. “It shouldn’t matter that you’re first,” Kra said. “Speed should not be a priority. It’s not about the proof production anymore. We need to find other ways to assess understanding.” However, “We can throw away priority, but people are going to want to be pioneers,” Hopkins countered, noting the challenge that mathematicians will now face in making in-roads where AI has already clear-cut.  Kra, however, struck a hopeful counterpoint:  “You can be a pioneer in different ways, for instance in communicating [how a proof came to be],” said Kra, who helped this year to draft the Leiden Declaration on Artificial Intelligence and Mathematics — a statement signed by mathematicians around the world that calls for action to address the risks that AI poses to mathematical research. “Communication of math is even more important now.”  Indeed, the panelists have already seen a subtle shift in what is expected of a mathematician, at all levels, from undergraduate students to early and established career mathematicians.  “The interview is becoming more important,” said Kra, noting that it’s no longer enough to accept, hire, or promote a mathematician based on ideas they have written or published — they have to also show that they understand and can explain those ideas to another person.  Human math AI is also making mathematicians question the role of academic journals, which have long been the benchmark for evaluating and validating mathematical advances. “Ninety percent of how we’ve judged [mathematicians] are through journals,” says Jacopo Borga, who is an early-career mathematician at MIT. “I’m not sure that’s how we should do this anymore. We should come up with a new metric and let it evolve.” Kra, who is a managing editor of a specialty journal, is seeing a huge increase in the number of papers submitted, primarily reporting results that were generated or assisted by AI. To deal with the deluge, that particular journal has had to hire an additional managing editor.  Where journal editors have traditionally prioritized publishing new proofs that push the field forward, Kra sees that, in response to AI “slop,” some publications are putting more value on exposition — the section of a paper that explains the reasoning behind a conjecture or proof. For now, humans have the advantage over AI in communicating mathematical ideas. “There’s a real art to exposition, if you can explain something in a clear and elegant way,” Hopkins echoed.  Kra noted that there are experimental journals coming online now, that are designed to highlight uniquely human contributions to mathematics. For instance, there are journals that publish expositions, such as papers that explain an old result in a new way that modern mathematicians can understand. “There is a lot of opportunity to curate and translate knowledge,” said Hopkins, who shared that one of his students has been working to prove a theorem from the 1970s. The original language and construction from that decades-old theorem, he said, was just as foreign as some of AI’s proofs today.  In noting novel approaches journals are taking in response to AI, Kra also mentioned Mathematical Discourse , a new peer-reviewed “video journal” that will feature videos of people giving talks about mathematical research. The journal’s preliminary site states that “giving a mathematical talk captures the human side of mathematics in a unique way, and supporting these human aspects of our discipline will be ever more important in the coming years.” “A new kind of mathematician” The rise of AI may be hitting especially hard for students, who are still learning the fundamentals in the presence of so many AI shortcuts.  “Mathematics is probably the slowest science you can do,” said Borga, to appreciative laughs from the audience. “Students today are bombarded by [conflicting messages of] what they should do, and are overwhelmed. We need to give them space to learn.” How they should learn could be a matter of personal belief.  “There is a big faction of my group who are ‘AI vegans’ [people who do not use AI], while others are using it,” said Hopkins, who is finding ways to support both groups. He also highlighted one particular student, who seemed to be a sort of “horse whisperer of AI.” This student has good mathematical instincts, Hopkins said, but struggles with execution. They are motivated by curiosity, rather than being first to a solution, and have a way of prompting AI to produce interesting insights.  “This may be a new kind of mathematician,” Hopkins said.  As AI forces the field of mathematics to adapt and change its centuries-long ways of pursuing knowledge, Borga and others see the moment as a new beginning, rather than math’s end. “The castle is collapsing,” Borga says. “There’s open ground to explore.” “AI is going to affect everyone (beyond mathematicians),” said Buckmaster, who urged students to stay the course “rather than escape or jump ship to another field. … Think of new ways to be creative and communicate your ideas,” he said. “Just do what you love.” The panel discussion, co-sponsored by the Department of Mathematics, is the first of a planned series hosted by MITHIC and SERC exploring how AI is reshaping our personal and professional lives.
